notes.1a: This is an example of a good, straightforward answer that took very little time and allowed the candidate to move quickly on to the next question: ‘ 14.2 × 0.76 = $10.792 billion’. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0455 Economics November 2022 This is an example of an unnecessarily complicated calculation that produced an incorrect answer and wasted time that could have been used answering other questions: ‘14.2 billion = 14, 200, 000, 000. 14 200 000 000 ÷ 100 = 142 000 000. 142 000 000 × 76 = 107 920 000 000 tertiary sector value’ It is very easy to become confused by the sheer number of zeros when working in billions and here the answer is incorrect because it contains one too many zeros. Candidates are strongly advised to avoid converting billions to numbers of ten or more digits and to keep the word ‘billion’ in their working instead. The correct answer to this question is $10.792 billion but one (10.8 bn) or two decimal places (10.79 bn) is acceptable. Unfortunately a number of candidates gave the answer as $10.7 bn but this is not strictly correct when rounded to one decimal place. Working in mathematical notation (powers of 10) is not necessary in questions such as this.
notes.1b: There was generally a good understanding of primary and tertiary sectors of the economy demonstrated in answers. The main problem seen in answers was a confusion of manufacturing (secondary) and service (tertiary) sectors shown by some candidates.
notes.1c: This question was very well answered, with most candidates able to identify increased life expectancy and falling infant mortality rates from the source material.
notes.1d: Similarly, most candidates found it a straightforward task to identify two reasons why millions of tourists visit Mauritius, such as tourist attractions and no visa requirements, going on to explain these points by giving the example of beautiful beaches and the easiness or low cost of travel to Mauritius.
notes.1e: Although candidates were generally successful at identifying two advantages of a firm setting up in Mauritius, there was often a problem here with identifying too many advantages and not explaining them fully. The question requires two advantages to be explained, with fast growth and political stability (from the source material) being two of them. Unfortunately many candidates treated this as a single advantage, when in fact they are separate issues, and then identified a third advantage – ‘also few regulations’. Only two advantages were asked for in the question and ‘also’ implies more than two here.
notes.1f: ‘ Percentage of international trade to GDP and GDP per head has a positive relationship. As percentage of international trade to GDP increases, so does GDP per head. Luxembourg has the highest percentage of international trade to GDP and the highest GDP per head. However Kenya has the lowest percentage with 33 per cent and the lowest has the lowest GDP per head with $187. However Mauritius is an exception because it has a higher percentage than Qatar but much lower GDP per head than Qatar.’ This is an excellent example of an answer to this question which is concise but covers the analysis comprehensively by using the source material well. It gives a simple overview (positive relationship), then identifies Luxembourg as the highest in both categories and Kenya as the lowest in both as supporting evidence of the relationship. The exception of Mauritius to this pattern is then identified and explained by comparing the figures to those of Qatar. No further analysis is therefore required. On the other hand, many candidates simply take figures from the data but provide no analysis of them, e.g. ‘ Luxembourg has a GDP per head of $114,704 with a percentage figure of 382 per cent’ . This is not analysing the data and cannot therefore be rewarded. External information not given in the table, such as the population or development status of the five selected countries, was rewarded if it was accurate and relevant but was not successful when vague and speculative.
notes.1g: This question was well answered, with candidates able to use the source material to observe that outward investment enables firms to enter new markets, to increase their revenues and profits, while importing products at a lower cost. They could then look at the other side of the discussion by commenting that these profits might not be reinvested back to help the home country and that this involved opportunity costs. As observed in the key comments above, the main weakness in answers was to answer with regard to the economy or government rather than a firm.
notes.1h: As with Question 1g , this question proved straightforward for candidates who used the source material appropriately. Good answers considered the benefits of infrastructure spending in terms of Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0455 Economics November 2022 boosting job opportunities, investment and economic growth, whilst boosting tourism was mentioned by nearly every candidate. This was contrasted with the dangers from demand-pull inflation and the opportunity costs in terms of spending on other government priorities, such as education. The main weakness seen in answers was focusing on firms rather than the Mauritian economy, as required by the question. Section B
notes.2a: The best answers were brief and to the point, contrasting the supply of an individual firm with the total supply of all the firms in the market. Weaker answers tended to be vague and give individual supply as being from one person (rather than one firm) and market supply as lots of people supplying (rather than firms).
notes.2b: Good answers used the ideas of geographical mobility and occupational mobility to give examples of how, for example, availability of transport and workplace skills respectively would influence mobility of labour. Weaker answers usually concentrated on the demand for labour from firms rather than the supply of labour by workers.
notes.2c: As noted in the key comments above, candidates often answered a different question, analysing the benefits of small firms to the economy rather than reasons for their existence. It was difficult for this approach to gain reward. The best answers were those where the idea of limitations to growth were analysed, such as lack of incentives and lack of available capital. The most popular approach was to refer to the idea that the owners of small firms preferred to maintain control by remaining small and keeping the firm ‘within the family’.
notes.2d: The following is an example of an answer that is clearly a Level 3 (L3) response because it is a reasoned discussion that considers both sides of the question. The first half is a little stronger than the second half because there is more depth, but only one aspect (inflation) is discussed in the second half, and the very last part of the answer is unclear: ‘A reduction in unemployment rate may benefit the economy because you are making use of more of the resources you have available so there is actual economic growth (production increase as well) (L1) . As less people are unemployed they do not take unemployment benefits, so there is a decrease in government expenditure (L2) which can enable the government to use that money in other things that benefit the economy, such as education. As less people are unemployed they gain an income which they can use to consume, so consumption increases, so firms increase their output to supply this increase in demand, so investment increases. All this causes aggregate demand to increase. But on the other hand this increase in aggregate demand may cause demand-pull inflation (L3) as firms cannot increase more their production with the increase in demand (it may be caused because all the unemployed had become employed) which cause an increase in price so consumption decreases, which may finally cause a decrease in aggregate demand and in actual economic growth’ ( L3 ) overall.
notes.3a: Most candidates provided a satisfactory definition of inflation for two marks. The idea of rising price was usually understood but time was mentioned less often, and the ‘general level’ was frequently missed in answers. The weakest answers referred to the price of a product rather than prices in general.
notes.3b: The most successful candidates stuck to the question, which was fundamentally about the low confidence individuals may have regarding their own economic situation. These candidates then gave straightforward answers about reduced spending and reduced borrowing as a result of this low confidence in the economy, backing this up by explaining that consumers would save instead and that they would be concerned about the risks of borrowing. Many other candidates instead deviated from the question to consider influences on spending and borrowing apart from low confidence. notes.3c: Good answers started with the basic macroeconomic aims (economic growth, low inflation, full employment, and balance of payments) and examined how conflicts could arise. The most popular approach was to explain how interest rate cuts would boost borrowing and thus consumption and total demand in the economy, whilst at the same time reducing saving. This in turn, however, could fuel demand-pull inflation, which conflicts with a macroeconomic aim outlined earlier. The best answers also explained that the extra demand could be for imports, worsening the current account situation. Less good answers strayed in a confused way into the impact of interest rate cuts upon banks and the government, sometimes arguing that the government would lose out because they would not earn as much interest as they previously had and that that would mean less spending on public services.
notes.3d: The following is a response that has Level 1 identifications of economic concepts but does not develop these ideas any further in order to reach Level 2. For example, inflation being caused is indicated but not explained, and certainty is identified but its importance is not developed further: ‘A country can benefit but also be damaged by a fixed foreign exchange rate system. It can have problems since it is attached to only one fixed number and it can not change it. This makes monetary policy worthless as they can not change the price of the exchange rate (L1) . This could cause inflation. However countries could benefit as they have a more clear and certain price always on imports and exports (L1) as prices do not change’. (L1) overall. The best answers explained the significance of the level at which the exchange rate had been fixed – too high or too low. For example, the argument that a fixed exchange rate could cause inflation was better if related to an exchange rate that was too low.
notes.4a: This question was generally well answered, with environmental protection by far the most popular answer given. There were, however, some excellent answers that considered other issues, such as support for charitable work and providing housing for workers.
notes.4b: Candidates who gave a simple, clearly structured answer to this question were by far the most successful. It was a straightforward task to identify two types of merger, e.g. horizontal and vertical, and then explain them by reference to the appropriate stages or sectors of production. Candidates who found this question problematic tended to produce long answers without reference to specific types of merger.
notes.4c: There was a significant split between those candidates who were comfortable with drawing and labelling diagrams accurately and those for whom their diagrams were inaccurate or demonstrated a lack of care. Candidates who appeared to understand the economics often missed out on marks because they did not label the axes, curves, or equilibrium points at all, or labelled them incorrectly. The best answers were those that were thorough in the presentation of the diagram and then commented precisely on the increased demand for solar energy and the subsequent rise in its price and/or quantity. It is important for candidates to be aware that describing the diagram is not the same as analysing it: to say ‘the demand curve moves to the right’ is insufficient, whereas ‘demand for solar energy increases’ is an appropriate comment.
notes.4d: The following is an example of a Level 3 (L3) response to this question about whether a merger can help a firm survive. Its strength lies not in its length but in the way that the discussion is developed concisely, and without deviating from the topic. It would have been even better if it had included specific mention of economies of scale as an aid to survival, although they are implied: ‘A merger can help a firm survive because it allows them to have a large diversity of products (L1) . This means that if a product loses its demand, the firm would still have other products to sell and avoid losing their revenues (L2) . A merger also helps them to reduce costs as they can get rid of duplicate assets meaning that costs of production will decrease, allowing them to charge lower prices to consumers while still being profitable and compete in the market. However the firm could suffer from diseconomies of scale if it grows too large. (L3) For example its large scale could become costly to handle. Workers may also become demotivated causing a reduction in productivity and output. Also the firm may lose its focus if they attempt to produce an incredibly Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0455 Economics November 2022 wide variety of goods and services, which could affect its quality as they would be focusing on more of what they can handle’. (L3) overall.
notes.5a: This question was quite well answered, with a clear understanding by most candidates that regulations are rules or laws imposed by the government. Some other candidates lacked a clear idea about the nature of regulations. They often gave taxation, including tariffs, as an answer but these are methods using changes to prices of products to influence behaviour in a market, rather than using rules or laws.
notes.5b: Candidates who understood the nature of ‘the quantity of labour’ had little difficulty in identifying two causes of its fall and explaining them. Good answers identified factors such as high death rates or increased emigration, and there were also some impressive topical references to war and pandemics reducing the population and hence reducing the workforce. Other candidates mistakenly took the quantity of labour to be the level of employment and therefore answered the question in terms of a fall in employment or a rise in unemployment. The quantity of labour (the labour force) includes the unemployed (those seeking work) as well as the employed.
notes.5c: Comprehensive answers to this question were rare, chiefly because most candidates did not develop their answers beyond pointing out that profits would be affected, either adversely or positively, and that investment was likely to increase if corporation tax was low. The better answers went beyond identifying these effects and explained how they could affect multinational companies, such as how a low corporation tax and increased profits could lead not only to increased investment but also to increased output and productivity. Very few candidates mentioned the effect on government revenue from corporation tax, where revenue from a high rate of tax might result in more expenditure on education and training, thus benefiting the MNCs in terms of the availability of skilled labour.
notes.5d: The following is a good Level 2 response to this question about the possible harm to an economy from falling economic growth. It does not quite reach Level 3 because there is insufficient use of economic analysis and not enough development of the issues identified: ‘A decrease in a country’s economic growth rate could harm its economy since it could lead to a recession. This means there would be less disposable income for consumers, (L1) decreasing demand and therefore affecting the economy. If the country is doing badly already, then a decrease in the economic growth rate would pull it down further. A decrease in the economic growth rate can decrease confidence within the country, decreasing investment (L2) and harming firms in the process. If there is less investment then firms would have less money to spend, which can result in firing workers to save money, increasing the number of unemployed. However, a decrease in a country’s economic growth rate would not always harm its economy because if the country was dealing with high inflation this could help it regulate back to its normal and stable place. A steady decrease in the rate of economic growth can help if the country’s prices were too high making them unaffordable to consumers so now they can purchase their products again. Plus, it gives time to firms that were struggling with the overpowering demand to come up with better alternatives and plans to control situations like this in the future. (L2) overall. As was the case with other part d responses, strong candidates often tended to under-perform in these discussion questions. This was basically because they did not produce enough, often having written longer answers for the much shorter questions. This could lead to a candidate running out of time and writing only a cursory answer for this last 8-mark question. As noted in the general comments above, time allocation is a very important skill for candidates to acquire and practise.
